notes:
Below are verse‑by‑verse notes for Genesis 36:23‑43, drawing on the pages I was able to read. Where a tradition‑specific view or a modern scholarly note was found, it is indicated. (I was unable to reach preceptaustin.org, Dr. Constable, the NET Bible notes, bibleodyssey.org, or any specifically Catholic/Orthodox/Word‑of‑Faith pages on this passage; those gaps are noted at the end.)

---

## Overview of the Passage

Genesis 36:23‑30 completes the genealogy of **Seir the Horite** (the pre‑Edomite cave‑dwelling inhabitants of Mount Seir). Verses 31‑39 list **eight early Edomite kings** who reigned “before any king reigned over the children of Israel.” Verses 40‑43 give a **second, territorial list of Edomite chiefs** (alluphîm). The whole chapter traces Esau’s line to show how God’s promise to Abraham (that kings would come from him, Gen 17:6) was partially fulfilled even in the non‑covenant line, while also documenting the people who would become persistent adversaries of Israel.

---

## Verse‑by‑Verse Notes

### v. 23 — “These are the sons of Shobal: Alvan, Manahath, Ebal, Shepho, and Onam.”

- **Shobal** was the second son of Seir the Horite (Gen 36:20). His five sons are listed here.
- The **name meanings** given by older lexicons (Gesenius, Fürst) are: **Alvan** = “unjust” or “lofty”; **Manahath** = “rest”; **Ebal** = “stripped of leaves” or “bare mountain”; **Shepho** = “nakedness”; **Onam** = “strong” (Pulpit Commentary).
- In the parallel list of 1 Chronicles 1:40, Alvan is called **Alian** and Shepho is called **Shephi** — minor spelling variations common in genealogical transmission (Gill).
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-36.html

### v. 24 — “These are the sons of Zibeon: Aiah and Anah. (This is the Anah who found the hot springs in the wilderness as he was pasturing the donkeys of his father Zibeon.)”

- **Zibeon** is a Horite chief, the grandfather of Esau’s wife Aholibamah (Gen 36:2, 25).
- The BSB renders the contested Hebrew word *yēmîm* as **“hot springs.”** The Pulpit Commentary notes that this is a *hapax legomenon* (a word occurring only once in Scripture). The traditional Jewish interpretation (followed by Luther, Calvin, Aben Ezra, Kimchi, and Adam Clarke) read it as “mules,” taking the verb *māṣāʾ* as “invented” (i.e., Anah first bred mules by crossing horses and donkeys). Modern scholarship rejects this because (a) *māṣāʾ* means “to find/discover,” not “to invent,” (b) horses were not yet present in that region, and (c) the text says Anah was tending only donkeys, not horses. The Vulgate and most modern commentators (Gesenius, Keil, Hengstenberg, Kalisch, Murphy) take it as **warm/hot springs**, of which several exist in the Edomite region (e.g., Callirrhoe in Wady Zerka Maein). (Pulpit Commentary; Ellicott notes the same.)
- **Ellicott** adds that Jerome said the Punic cognate word means “hot springs.”
- **Enduring Word** (David Guzik) simply notes that Anah “found the water,” assuming the “hot springs” reading without argument.
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-36.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-36.html ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-36/

### v. 25 — “These are the children of Anah: Dishon and Oholibamah daughter of Anah.”

- **Anah** here is the son of Zibeon (brother of Aiah), not to be confused with his uncle Anah mentioned in Gen 36:20.
- **Dishon** was named after his great‑uncle (Seir’s son Dishon/Dishan, v. 21).
- **Oholibamah** was not Esau’s wife but the **cousin** of Esau’s wife’s father — i.e., she shares the name with Esau’s Horite wife Aholibamah (who was the daughter of *this* Anah). (Pulpit Commentary)
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-36.html

### v. 26 — “These are the sons of Dishon: Hemdan, Eshban, Ithran, and Cheran.”

- **Dishon** here is the son of Seir (Gen 36:21). Name meanings: **Hemdan** = “pleasant” (Gesenius); **Eshban** = “reason/understanding” (Gesenius) or “intelligent/hero” (Fürst); **Ithran** = “the excellent one,” related to the names Jethro and Jithron (Gesenius, Fürst, Murphy, Lange); **Cheran** = “harp” (Gesenius) or “companion” (Fürst). (Pulpit Commentary)
- **David Guzik** notes that “Ithran” means “advantage,” and points out that many Edomite names do not reflect a godly heart. (Enduring Word)
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-36.html ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-36/

### v. 27 — “These are the sons of Ezer: Bilhan, Zaavan, and Akan.”

- **Ezer** = “treasure” (Gesenius). His three sons: **Bilhan** = “modest” (Gesenius) or “tender” (Fürst); **Zaavan** = “disturbed” (Gesenius); **Akan** (Jakan in 1 Chron 1:42) = “twisting” (Gesenius, Murphy). (Pulpit Commentary)
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-36.html

### v. 28 — “These are the sons of Dishan: Uz and Aran.”

- **Dishan** is the seventh son of Seir (the name is the same as Dishon; see Gen 36:21). **Uz** = “sandy” (Gesenius, Fürst); **Aran** = “wild goat” (Gesenius) or “power/strength” (Fürst). (Pulpit Commentary)
- **David Guzik** highlights the name **Aran** (“mountain goat”) as another name that does not reflect a godly heart. (Enduring Word)
- The name **Uz** also appears as the homeland of Job; some older commentators speculated a link, but most dismiss it.
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-36.html ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-36/

### vv. 29‑30 — “These are the chiefs of the Horites: Chiefs Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Dishon, Ezer, and Dishan. They are the chiefs of the Horites, according to their divisions in the land of Seir.”

- These seven are the **phylarchs** (tribal princes) of the Horite people who inhabited Seir before and alongside Esau’s descendants. The Pulpit Commentary notes that the Edomites gradually dispossessed and absorbed the Horites, as stated in Deuteronomy 2:12.
- The term “duke” (alluph) refers to a **tribal chief**, not a hereditary monarch. (Ellicott)
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-36.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-36.html

### v. 31 — “These are the kings who reigned in the land of Edom before any king reigned over the Israelites:”

- **This verse is a major crux for authorship debates.** The Pulpit Commentary outlines three positions:
  1. **Post‑Mosaic authorship or later interpolation** (Le Clerc, Bleek, Ewald, Adam Clarke, Lange) — the phrase “before any king reigned over the children of Israel” implies the writer lived after Saul’s monarchy.
  2. **Mosaic, referring to the prophetic promise** — Moses knew from Genesis 17:6 and 35:11 that kings would come from Jacob, and from Genesis 27:40 that Esau would also produce rulers. He is simply saying Edom achieved monarchy *before* Israel did, which was already true in his day (Calvin, Keil, Hengstenberg, Havernick).
  3. **Moses himself was “king in Jeshurun”** (Deut 33:5), so he could speak of Israel having a king (Gill).
- **Ellicott** strongly holds that the list is a later addition from the time of the monarchy, calling attempts to make it Mosaic “painful to read” and likely to “harden sceptics in unbelief.” He views it as a legitimate prophetic‑school addition.
- **StudyLight verse‑by‑verse** notes that “this reference to the kings to which their sister nation had submitted was a warning against the desires of the children of Israel to have kings” (following Kline and Francisco).
- The pattern of kingship was **elective, not hereditary** — no son succeeds his father, each king comes from a different city, suggesting either election by the dukes or successive usurpations. (Pulpit Commentary; Keil)
- URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/36-31.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-36.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-36.html

### v. 32 — “Bela son of Beor reigned in Edom; the name of his city was Dinhabah.”

- **Bela** = the same name as Zoar (Gen 14:2). His father **Beor** shares the name of Balaam’s father (Num 22:5), though no connection is claimed.
- **Dinhabah** = perhaps “concealment” or “place of plunder” (Gesenius). Its location is unknown. (Pulpit Commentary)
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-36.html

### v. 33 — “When Bela died, Jobab son of Zerah from Bozrah reigned in his place.”

- **Jobab** = possibly “desert” or “shout” (Gesenius). The **LXX identified him with Job**, but commentators broadly reject this — the names differ in derivation, and there is no positive evidence (Michaelis called it *insinis error*). David Guzik cites Adam Clarke: “Many have supposed that Jobab is the same as Job… but there is no proper proof of this, and there are many reasons against it.” (Enduring Word; Pulpit Commentary)
- **Bozrah** = “fort” (Gesenius), later a major Edomite city mentioned in Isaiah 34:6 and Jeremiah 49:13, traceable to modern El‑Busaireh in Arabia Petraea. (Pulpit Commentary)
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-36.html ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-36/

### v. 34 — “When Jobab died, Husham from the land of the Temanites reigned in his place.”

- **Husham** = “haste” (Gesenius), related to the name Hushai.
- **Teman** was a district in northern Idumea, named after a grandson of Esau (Gen 36:11), with a city of the same name (not yet discovered). (Pulpit Commentary)
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-36.html

### v. 35 — “When Husham died, Hadad son of Bedad, who defeated Midian in the country of Moab, reigned in his place. And the name of his city was Avith.”

- **Hadad** = “shouting” or “conqueror” (Fürst). His father **Bedad** = “separation” (Gesenius).
- His notable exploit was **defeating Midian in the field of Moab** — a victory about which all other memory has vanished, confirming the antiquity of the record (Ellicott).
- Some tried to identify this Hadad with the Edomite adversary of Solomon (1 Kgs 11:14), but the Pulpit Commentary gives four reasons why this is impossible: (1) Solomon’s Hadad was of royal blood; this one was not described as such; (2) this Hadad was a reigning king, Solomon’s was a pretender; (3) this Hadad fought Midianites, who had vanished by Solomon’s time; (4) this Hadad lived before Israel had any kings.
- **Avith** = “ruins” (Gesenius) or “hut‑village” (Fürst).
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-36.html

### v. 36 — “When Hadad died, Samlah from Masrekah reigned in his place.”

- **Samlah** = “covering” or “garment” (Gesenius, Fürst, Murphy).
- **Masrekah** = “vineyard” (Gesenius). (Pulpit Commentary)
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-36.html

### v. 37 — “When Samlah died, Shaul from Rehoboth on the Euphrates reigned in his place.”

- **Shaul** (Saul) = “asked” (Gesenius).
- **“Rehoboth on the Euphrates”** (literally “Rehoboth of the River”) — the Pulpit Commentary notes that Onkelos and Keil understand “the River” to be the Euphrates, which would place this Shaul’s origin far outside Edomite territory near the mouth of the Chaboras (Errachabi/Rachabeh). Lange, however, suggests it may be a smaller river (*nahar*) within Idumea, making the site uncertain. Ellicott adds that if it were the Euphrates, Shaul probably reigned in Idumea by right of conquest. It is distinguished from “Rehoboth Ir” in Gen 10:11.
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-36.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-36.html

### v. 38 — “When Shaul died, Baal‑hanan son of Achbor reigned in his place.”

- **Baal‑hanan** = “Lord of Benignity” or “lord of grace” (Gesenius). **David Guzik** notes that “his name embraced the false god Baal,” illustrating the non‑godly character of the Edomite line. (Enduring Word)
- **Achbor** = “mouse” (Gesenius).
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-36.html ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-36/

### v. 39 — “When Baal‑hanan son of Achbor died, Hadad reigned in his place. His city was named Pau, and his wife’s name was Mehetabel daughter of Matred, the daughter of Me‑zahab.”

- The BSB reads **Hadad** (following 1 Chron 1:50); the Masoretic text here reads **Hadar** — an easy scribal confusion of the Hebrew letters *r* (resh) and *d* (daleth) (Ellicott).
- **Pau** (Pai in 1 Chron 1:50) = “bleating” (Gesenius) or “yawning” (Fürst).
- **Mehetabel** = “whom God benefits” (Gesenius); **Matred** = “pushing” (Gesenius); **Me‑zahab** = “water of gold” (Gesenius).
- That Hadad’s death is **not recorded here** (unlike the previous seven kings) strongly suggests that he was **still alive when this list was composed.** Most conservative commentators identify him as the king of Edom to whom Moses sent messengers from Kadesh requesting passage through Edom (Num 20:14‑21). The later Chronicler adds “Hadad died also” (1 Chron 1:51). (Pulpit Commentary; Ellicott; Keil & Delitzsch)
- The unusual detail about his wife and her lineage may indicate that his rule carried particular dynastic significance, or simply that the compiler had more information about the currently reigning king.
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-36.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-36.html

### v. 40 — “These are the names of Esau’s chiefs, according to their families and regions, by their names: Chiefs Timna, Alvah, Jetheth,”

- This is a **territorial list** of Edomite chiefs (*alluphîm*), distinct from the earlier genealogical list of Esau’s grandsons (vv. 15‑19). Commentators agree these are not new individuals but names of **districts or settlements** named after chieftains — a political‑geographical catalogue of Edom in its final settled form. (Keil & Delitzsch; Ellicott; Pulpit Commentary)
- **Timna** — previously a female name (Gen 36:12, Lotan’s sister and Eliphaz’s concubine), now appears as a male chief or territorial name. Barnes notes “unless we allow a duchess in her own right to have occurred among them.”
- **Alvah** (or Aliah) is closely related to the name **Alvan** in v. 23.
- **Jetheth** = “nail” (Gesenius) or “subjugation” (Fürst) — a new name not seen earlier.
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-36.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/36-43.htm

### v. 41 — “Oholibamah, Elah, Pinon,”

- **Oholibamah** — like Timna, a female name now appearing in a male/territorial list. Possibly the region named after Esau’s Horite wife.
- **Elah** = “terebinth” (Murphy) or “strength” (Fürst). Identified by Keil as the port **Aila** (Elath) on the Gulf of Aqaba (cf. Gen 14:6).
- **Pinon** = probably “dark” (Gesenius). Identified as **Phunon**, an Israelite encampment (Num 33:42‑43), celebrated for its copper mines, between Petra and Zoar. (Keil & Delitzsch)
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-36.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/36-43.htm

### v. 42 — “Kenaz, Teman, Mibzar,”

- **Kenaz** and **Teman** are the only two names that **reappear** from the earlier list of Esau’s grandsons (Gen 36:11, 15) — meaning only these two original tribal districts survived the turbulent period of the kings and retained their identity in the later territorial arrangement. (Ellicott; Pulpit Commentary)
- **Mibzar** = “fortress” or “strong city” (Gesenius). Some (Knobel) identified it with Petra, but Keil notes Petra is elsewhere called **Selah** (2 Kgs 14:7).
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-36.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/36-43.htm

### v. 43 — “Magdiel, and Iram. These were the chiefs of Edom, according to their settlements in the land they possessed. Esau was the father of the Edomites.”

- **Magdiel** = “prince of God” (Gesenius). The Targum of Jonathan says this duke was called Magdiel from his city, which was a strong tower (*migdal*). Jerome located it in the country of Gabalena. Some later Jewish writers (e.g., Pirke Eliezer) identified Magdiel with **Rome**, seeing Esau/Edom as the ancestor of the Roman Empire (Gill).
- **Iram** = “citizen” or “naked” (Gesenius).
- **“According to their settlements in the land they possessed”** — Matthew Henry draws a pointed application: while the Israelites dwelt in bondage in Egypt with only the *promise* of Canaan, the Edomites already dwelt in their own habitations and possessed Seir. “The children of this world have their all in hand, and nothing in hope, while the children of God have often their all in hope, and next to nothing in hand. But, all things considered, it is better to have Canaan in promise than mount Seir in possession.” (Matthew Henry, via BibleHub)
- **“Esau was the father of the Edomites”** — the closing bracket of the chapter, reiterating that the great nation of Edom, with all its princes and kings, sprang from Esau. This prepares the narrative to turn back to Jacob’s line in Genesis 37. (Keil & Delitzsch)
- **Gill** adds a distinction: the former dukes (vv. 15‑19) were dukes *in* the land of Edom alongside Horite dukes; these later dukes are dukes *of* Edom, having driven out the Horites and become sole possessors and sovereign lords. Thus while Israel was a sojourner in a strange land, Esau’s family were possessors of a land they could call their own.
- URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/36-43.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-36/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-36.html

## Points of Difference Between Traditions

Given that Genesis 36 is largely genealogical, the major traditional differences centre on **v. 31** (“before any king reigned over the children of Israel”) and **v. 24** (the meaning of *yēmîm*):

### v. 31 — Authorship and Dating

- **Conservative Reformed / Lutheran / traditional Mosaic authorship defenders** (represented by Calvin, Keil, Hengstenberg, Havernick in the Pulpit Commentary notes): Moses wrote v. 31 with the *prophetic promise* of Genesis 35:11 and 17:6 in view. He is not looking back from the time of Saul, but stating a fact already true in his day — Edom got kings before Israel did. Moses himself functioned as “king in Jeshurun” (Deut 33:5), so “before any king reigned over Israel” can be a Mosaic statement. (Pulpit Commentary; StudyLight verse‑by‑verse page)
- **Anglican / critical scholarship** (Ellicott): The plain sense is that the writer lived after the Israelite monarchy was established. Ellicott calls attempts to make it Mosaic “painful to read” and believes the list was added by the prophetic schools during the time of Samuel or the early monarchy — a legitimate, inspired editorial addition to the sacred text, not a corruption. (Ellicott)
- **Some Baptists / Evangelicals** (Adam Clarke, cited by several sources): The entire king list (vv. 31‑39) was a post‑Mosaic insertion from 1 Chronicles 1:43‑50, perhaps originally a marginal note that a later copyist incorporated into the text. (Pulpit Commentary; StudyLight)

### v. 24 — “Found the hot springs” vs. “found the mules”

- **Traditional Protestant reading (Luther, Calvin, many older commentators):** Anah “found the mules” — i.e., he was the first to breed mules by crossing horses and donkeys. This reading was standard in the Reformation era.
- **Modern conservative / evangelical reading (Keil, Hengstenberg, most modern commentators):** The Hebrew word *yēmîm* means “hot springs” (supported by the Vulgate’s *aquas calidas*, by cognate evidence from Punic cited by Jerome, and by the known existence of thermal springs in the region). Enduring Word (David Guzik) adopts this reading without controversy, translating “found the water.”
- The Pulpit Commentary surveys both views at length and concludes decisively for “hot springs.” The same conclusion is found in Barnes’ Notes on the Bible (via BibleHub).
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-36.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-36.html
